FOR INDEPENDENT WEDDING & EVENT PHOTOGRAPHERS

A flat add-on price can still be a losing job.

Charging $300 for an extra hour reads fine right up until the culling and editing hours it generates, the gear wear, and any second-shooter payout come out of it. This free calculator finds real net profit for one add-on, then lets you compare two or three options by what they actually pay per hour of your own time — not their headline price.

Everything on this page runs in your browser and nothing is ever uploaded. Your add-on inputs (time, second-shooter and gear costs, price) are saved locally on this device so you don't retype them next time — Reset to defaults clears them, and Copy shareable link puts them in a URL fragment your browser never sends anywhere. Your comparison rows are a different promise: they are never saved anywhere, and closing or refreshing the tab clears them. There is no account. We count only anonymous local feature events (addon-priced, addons-compared, link-copied, reset) so we can tell whether the calculator gets used — no add-on names, prices, or figures are recorded, and Do Not Track / Global Privacy Control turn it off automatically.

Add-on looks fine on paper — is it actually worth it?

A $450 second-shooter add-on can pay less than the extra hour it took to charge for it, once the culling, editing, and subcontractor fee are netted out. Is a second shooter worth it? works through the arithmetic on a real underpriced add-on next to a solid one.

Common questions

Why does a flat add-on price not tell me whether it's worth offering?

Because the flat price is usually set by comparing to what other studios charge, not by counting what the add-on actually costs. Culling and editing an extra hour of coverage, or a second shooter's entire take, routinely runs to one to two times the shoot hours that produced it -- time that never shows up on an invoice the way a subcontractor payment does, but is just as real.

Does this tool write my client contract or tell me what to charge?

No. This calculator only prices your own add-on economics from numbers you supply. It does not do tax planning, business-entity formation, or contract review, and it does not replace a signed client contract, your own liability or gear insurance, or your accountant.

Why does my own time count as a cost when no cash actually changes hands?

Because your target hourly rate is what you have decided your time is worth, and an add-on that pays less than that rate is quietly cutting your own pay to take it. Counting only cash costs like a second shooter's fee or an album vendor's bill -- and not your own culling and editing hours -- is the most common way an add-on's real profit gets overstated.

Does anything about my add-on or comparison rows get uploaded?

No. Every field on this page runs in your browser only. Nothing is sent to a server, there is no account, and the add-on rows you type into the comparison table are never saved anywhere -- they exist only in the page while it is open. The add-on inputs above are different: those are saved locally on this device, so you don't retype them, and a shareable link can carry them to another device. Usage counting only tallies anonymous feature events, and you can turn it off with the button above.

is-a-second-shooter-worth-it.html.text:
← Back to the photo package add-on pricing calculator

Is a second shooter worth it?

An add-on reads as one number — "$300 for an extra hour" or "$450 for a second shooter" — and that number is the one thing it does not tell you: how much the add-on actually pays once you count what it takes to deliver it. Two real-shaped add-ons below, run through the same arithmetic, end up in very different places.

The solid add-on: an extra hour of coverage

Target hourly rate $75. One extra shoot hour, plus half an hour of culling and an hour and a half of editing the extra images it generates — three hours of the photographer's own time. A $5 gear wear allowance, no subcontractor and no physical goods, charged at $300.

Amount
Gross revenue$300.00
Your labor cost (at target rate)$225.00
Total cost$230.00
Net profit$70.00
Effective hourly rate$23.33/hr
Profit margin23.3%

This add-on pays the photographer's full target rate for all three hours, plus another $23.33/hr on top — a genuinely profitable add-on, not just one that "sounds fine."

The underpriced add-on: a second shooter at $450

Same target hourly rate. No extra shoot hours for the primary photographer, but the second shooter's take adds an hour and a half of culling and two hours of editing — three and a half hours of the primary photographer's own time. A $250 fee paid to the second shooter and a $10 gear wear allowance for the extra body, charged at $450 — a number that sounds like it should easily cover a $250 payout.

Amount
Gross revenue$450.00
Your labor cost (at target rate)$262.50
Total cost$522.50
Net profit-$72.50
Effective hourly rate-$20.71/hr
Profit margin-16.1%

-$72.50 and a -16.1% margin are a loss, not a rounding error: this add-on's own cost — the second shooter's fee, the gear wear, and 3.5 hours of the primary photographer's own culling and editing valued at their own target rate — adds up to more than the $450 charged. A photographer who only checks "does $450 cover the $250 I'm paying the second shooter" keeps taking these.

The difference is culling, editing, and the subcontractor fee — not the headline price

$150 separated these two add-on prices, and $44.05/hr separated what they actually paid. The second shooter's own fee is easy to check against the price charged; the primary photographer's own extra culling and editing hours are not, because nothing invoices for them. Run your own numbers before you set a second-shooter price from what other studios charge rather than from what the add-on actually costs you.

Common questions

Why does the second-shooter add-on show a loss if clients are happy to pay $450 for it?

Because none of its costs disappeared -- the extra culling and editing hours, the subcontractor fee, and the gear wear apply no matter what the client is happy to pay. Together they cost more than the $450 charged, which the headline price alone never shows.

What is the fastest way to tell two add-ons apart?

Compare effective hourly rate, not the headline price. The extra-hour add-on pays about $23.33/hr above target on this booking; the second-shooter add-on pays about -$20.71/hr for a costlier version of the same booking -- a $150 gap in price hides a $44.05/hr gap in what the add-on actually paid.

vs-pricing-by-comparing-to-other-studios.text:
← Photo Package Add-On Pricing Calculator

This calculator vs. pricing an add-on by comparing to what other studios charge

Most add-on prices come from one place: what other studios in the area charge for the same thing. That number answers whether a client will accept the price. It says nothing about whether the price covers this studio's own culling and editing hours, gear wear, and any subcontractor or physical-goods cost — and two studios charging the identical $300 for an extra hour can end up with completely different profit on it.

What each approach actually answers

Comparing to what other studios charge answers "will a client pay this?" — a real and necessary question, because a price nobody accepts never gets booked at all. It has no visibility into this studio's own numbers: how many culling and editing hours this specific add-on generates, whether a second shooter or an album vendor gets paid out of it, or what gear wear it puts on a body or lens.

This calculator answers a different question: "does this studio actually profit at this price, after its own time and costs?" It takes the photographer's target hourly rate, the extra shoot/cull/edit hours the add-on generates, any second-shooter or physical-goods cost, and a gear wear allowance, and returns net profit and effective hourly rate for the price being considered — then lets several add-on options be ranked by effective hourly rate instead of headline price.

Neither replaces the other. A price that clears both — competitive against comparable studios and profitable on this studio's own cost structure — is the one actually worth offering.

Two questions, two answers

QuestionWhere to answer it
Will a client accept this add-on's price?Checking what comparable studios charge — this calculator has no data on that.
Does this studio actually profit at that price?This calculator — free, private, from your own numbers.
Which of two or three add-on options pays best per hour of my own time?This calculator's comparison table, ranked by effective hourly rate.
Is my pricing data uploaded anywhere?No. Everything runs in your browser; your figures stay on this device.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and nothing you type is uploaded anywhere.

Common questions

Isn't matching what other studios charge a reasonable way to price an add-on?

It tells a client the price is competitive, which matters for booking the add-on at all. It says nothing about whether that price covers this studio's own culling and editing hours, gear wear, and any subcontractor or physical-goods cost -- two studios can charge the same $300 for an extra hour and have completely different profit on it, because their own cull/edit time and costs differ. Competitive pricing and profitable pricing are two different questions, and only one of them is answered by checking what other studios charge.

So should this studio ignore what other studios charge?

No -- it is still useful for setting a price a client will accept. The point is that it is only half the picture. Checking a competitor's price answers "will a client pay this?"; running the same price through this calculator answers "does this studio actually profit at this price, after its own time and costs?" Both questions matter, and only one of them needs a competitor's number at all.

What does a market-rate price hide that this calculator would catch?

The culling and editing hours an add-on generates, most often. A second shooter's take or an extra hour of coverage routinely produces one to two times the shoot hours in post-production time, and that time never appears on an invoice the way a subcontractor payment does -- so a price that looks competitive against another studio's rate card can still pay the photographer less than their own target hourly rate once those hours are counted.

Does this replace checking what other studios in the area actually charge?

No, and it is not built to. This calculator only prices this studio's own add-on economics from numbers supplied to it -- it has no data on what any other studio charges, and does not attempt to estimate a competitive market rate. Checking comparable studios' pricing is still worth doing; it just answers a different question than this calculator does.
